concept.name: Time-series momentum
concept.definition: A strategy that takes long positions in assets whose own trailing return is positive and short positions where it is negative - each asset against its own history rather than against peers - typically with volatility-scaled sizing. Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen (2012) document significant time-series momentum across 58 liquid futures in equity indexes, currencies, commodities, and bonds, persisting about a year and partially reversing thereafter.
concept.intuition: Do not ask whether gold beat stocks; ask whether gold beat gold - if its own past year is up, be long, if down, be short, and size each bet so every market contributes equal risk.
concept.mechanics: For each instrument, take the sign of the past 12-month excess return as the direction (long if positive, short if negative), size positions inversely to ex-ante volatility (estimated from exponentially weighted squared daily returns with a 60-day center of mass), and hold one month, averaging returns across cohorts. The diversified factor has little exposure to standard asset-pricing factors and performs best during extreme markets.
concept.formula: Per-instrument TSMOM return = sign(r_{t-12..t-1}) x (40% / sigma_{t-1}) x r_t, with sigma^2 = 261 x sum_i (1-delta) delta^i (r_{t-1-i} - r_bar)^2.
concept.failure_modes: Whipsawing ranges reverse the sign of trailing returns repeatedly, and sharp V-shaped reversals hit the strategy exactly when it is maximally positioned for the prior trend; crowding among trend-following funds compresses the effect out of sample.
concept.misconceptions: That it is the same thing as cross-sectional momentum; time-series momentum uses an asset's own past return with no winner/loser ranking, and empirically it largely subsumes the cross-sectional stock effect while remaining a distinct construction.
concept.example: Crude oil's trailing 12-month excess return is +18% with ex-ante volatility of 30%: go long sized at 40%/30% = 1.33 volatility units; natural gas at 60% volatility gets half that size, so both positions contribute equal risk.

citations.source: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen, 'Time Series Momentum', Journal of Financial Economics 104(2), 2012, 228-250 (author-hosted PDF, NYU Stern)
